bio.en: Jonathan Lowenhar runs Enjoy The Work, a firm whose singular mission is to help founders become great CEOs, through mentoring and advising rooted in the study of how the best startups operate.
bio.zh: Jonathan Lowenhar 经营着 Enjoy The Work，这家公司唯一的使命是帮助创始人成为杰出的 CEO，其辅导与咨询建立在“研究最优秀初创公司如何运作”之上。

summary.en: Jonathan draws a sharp line between being a founder (a state of being) and being a CEO (a craft), and pushes back on 'founder mode' as an excuse for not learning the job—the best CEOs know when to calibrate between the two. He walks through the two phases of a startup (build something people want; then build a company around it), the most common CEO failure modes, and his 'Magic Box' paradigm for a successful exit (never be 'for sale'—seduce the buyer instead). The episode is full of advice on hiring, building a repeatable go-to-market motion, and trusting your intuition as a founder.
summary.zh: Jonathan 划清了“创始人”（一种存在状态）与“CEO”（一门手艺）的界限，并批评“创始人模式”成了不学本分的借口——最优秀的 CEO 知道何时在两者间切换。他拆解了创业的两个阶段（做出人们想买的东西；再围绕它建一家公司）、最常见的 CEO 失败模式，以及他用于成功退出的“Magic Box”范式（永远不要“待售”——而要 seduce 买方）。这期节目充满关于招聘、打造可复制的上市动作、以及作为创始人学会信任直觉的建议。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something you talk about, there's these two phases to a startup journey and most people focus on the first phase.
turns.zh: 你提到的初创公司发展有两个阶段，大多数人只关注第一个阶段。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: Phase one is build something people want to buy. Phase two, the one we don't talk about is now you have to build a company around that thing people want to buy. Building a company is always the same. I don't care if it's MedTech or fintech or hardware or consumer.
turns.zh: 第一个阶段是打造人们愿意购买的产品。第二个阶段——我们不常谈论的阶段——是围绕这个产品建立一家公司。建立公司的过程始终如一。无论是医疗科技、金融科技、硬件还是消费品行业，都适用同样的法则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've come up with this methodology that you call the Magic Box paradigm that helps founders think about how to lead to a successful exit long-term.
turns.zh: 你提出了一个名为“魔法盒范式”的方法，帮助创始人思考如何实现长期成功退出。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: This is a traditional sales process. You build a list of the companies that might want to acquire you, you ping them and you hope you get a deal. Magic Box argues that the best outcomes for early-stage startups don't happen that way. You're never for sale. In fact, you have seduced a buyer. They see the fantasy, they fall in love.
turns.zh: 传统的销售流程是这样操作的：列出可能收购你的公司名单，主动联系他们，然后期待达成交易。魔法盒范式认为，这并非初创公司早期阶段的最佳路径。你永远不应把自己出售给别人。事实上，你要去勾引买家。让他们看到美好的愿景，坠入爱河。

How do they learn how to run a company well? I started to ask investors obsessively, and I asked them, Lenny, I asked them all three questions, same three over and over and over again. (00:05:14): First question was, well, describe to me your ideal founder. What's a great founder? The answers universally were the same. Investors would use words that meant grit and tenacity and courage and insight, and I'd say, "Great. Question number two, describe to me a great startup CEO," and they use none of those words. How can that possibly be true? Instead, they describe skills. This is a person who knows how to build stuff and sell stuff and recruit people and raise capital and organize humans and financially plan. Question number three, my final one, well, how does a founder learn those skills while doing the job? I got blank fucking stares, over and over again. It led me down this path that I'm now 10 years into with my colleagues of, well, how do we help founders learn those skills so that their venture investors don't fire them, so that they can actually go build whatever company they want to build and stay in the job for as long as they want to stay in the job? That's origin, that's what got me going.
turns.zh: 我经营过许多不同类型的公司，它们截然不同。我曾为一家上市公司管理过大型部门，后来担任私募股权公司的首席执行官，接着连续创办了两家初创企业。第一家进展不顺，但最终被出售；第二家则发展得相当不错。当我离开第二家公司时，和许多创业者一样，我健康状况极差，体重超重25磅，睡眠不足，诸多问题缠身。我花了几个月时间恢复健康，然后回顾自己职业生涯中的这些经历。当时我注意到一个现象：所有运营良好的公司，无论是上市公司、私募股权公司、初创企业，还是处于早期或成长期的公司，运作模式都极为相似。这怎么可能呢？当这些公司运营得当时，它们的运作方式为何如此惊人地一致？（00:04:35）我开始痴迷于这个问题，最终意识到每个成功的公司都有一种节奏感。这是无法忽视的存在，你不可能错过它，也无法忽视它。只要花几天时间通过隐蔽摄像头观察一家企业，你就能发现这种模式。为什么有些初创企业能成功，有些则不行？创始人如何才能掌握这种节奏感？他们如何学会有效运营一家公司？我开始反复询问投资者，问他们三个相同的问题：（00:05:14）第一个问题是，描述一下你理想中的创始人是什么样的。优秀的创始人应该具备哪些特质？答案普遍一致——他们会提及坚韧、勇气、洞察力等品质。我接着问：“很好，那第二个问题，描述一下优秀的初创企业CEO应该具备哪些特质？”他们却不再提及这些品质，而是列举了构建产品、销售产品、招募人才、融资、组织团队和财务规划等技能。最后一个问题：创始人如何在实际工作中习得这些技能？得到的都是茫然的注视。由此引发了我的十年探索——如何帮助创始人掌握这些技能，让风险投资人不再迫使他们离职，让他们能够专注于打造理想的公司，并长期留任？这就是Origin的初心所在，也是我持续探索的动力。

They can drop into a product feature, they can drop into a customer conversation or a partner conversation or with a long-time employee that's still in IC and be impactful and then rise back up if they've gone the training and get back into a cockpit to run the company again. That's to me the distinction. It's not manager mode is bad, it's the greatest CEOs know when to calibrate which one is needed.
turns.zh: 这感觉像个借口。我们给创始人许可，不让他们学习如何做好本职工作。想象一下一家正在崛起的初创公司，会有这样一个阶段：我必须发明一些东西。现在我要想办法让客户接触到这项发明，看看是否有效，然后围绕它建立商业模式，寻找可重复的吸引、转化和让客户满意的方法。接着，我得去创造大量需求，再建立一个能处理所有需求的运营体系。哦，对了，还要在某个时候把正向收入转化为正向现金流。文章暗示创始人只要自己写代码，就无需提升技能去掌握这些能力，甚至认为学习这些能力是负面的，这简直太荒谬了。（00:10:52）：创办公司需要的能力与发展公司、扩大规模、退出等阶段不同，最优秀的初创公司CEO会一路学习这些能力。学习方式多种多样。我不是说只有一条路，但创始人模式几乎成了不去学习的借口。我认为创始人独特之处在于，与被空降进来的职业经理人CEO不同，创始人了解公司从无到有的全过程。他们能以最细致的层面介入任何环节——产品功能、客户对话、合作伙伴沟通，甚至与仍在IC的长期员工交流，产生影响力，然后再回归管理岗位。这才是区别所在。管理者模式并非糟糕，而是最优秀的CEO知道何时调整所需模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I'm glad we got there. I wasn't planning to talk about founder mode, but I think this is really helpful for folks to hear that are founders and people working for founders too. Along these same lines, you have a really helpful and really funny also mental model for how to think about common failure modes of founders. You have these labels that I love, and this is actually the first thing I heard about Enjoy The Work is these labels that you guys use, and you also, a similar mental model for failure modes for a startup. Can you just share these modes that you've come up with?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这点了。很高兴我们能探讨这个话题。我本没打算谈创始人模式，但我觉得这对创始人以及为创始人工作的伙伴们都很有帮助。顺着这个思路，你还有一个非常实用且有趣的心智模型，用来思考创始人常见的失败模式。你提到的那些标签太棒了，这是我第一次听说Enjoy The Work团队用这些标签，还有你为初创公司失败模式设计的类似心智模型。能分享一下你总结的这些模式吗？

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: We do take a bit of a comical approach to some of this. As I've shared with you previously, the name of our company is not an accident. If we can't be playful, we can take the work seriously and not ourselves, so we do fuck around quite a bit. I think if I would separate failure modes for companies versus CEOs for a minute, the company ones are not quite as comedic, but they are ones we see all the time. One is you chose the wrong market. I don't think we need to belabor that one. Lots of your prior guests have talked about the importance of getting that part right or nothing else really matters. (00:13:05): Second, back to what we were discussing a minute ago, build something people want to buy, got to go build the right thing. Cool. Third one, founder's function. We like to joke that more companies die from suicide than homicide, and it's grim, but also if the two or three people in charge of the business can't get along, nothing else matters. It's all going to break apart. Then fourth, execution, and execution now leads back to CEO. Okay, so now we have a bunch of playful ones here. We have the robot CEO, who believes emotion should not ever exist at a startup, at which point we train them on a very simple formula. Emotions are messy, humans have emotions, startups need humans, therefore startups are messy.
turns.zh: 我们的确对某些事情采取了有点搞笑的处理方式。正如我之前跟你们分享的，我们公司的名字并非偶然之作。如果我们不能保持轻松的心态，至少可以认真对待工作，但不必太把自己当回事，所以我们确实经常开开玩笑。我觉得如果把公司和CEO的失败模式分开讲，公司的失败模式没那么搞笑，但却是我们常见的现象。第一种是选错了市场。我觉得这点无需多言。你们之前邀请的很多嘉宾都强调，选对市场至关重要，否则其他一切都无从谈起。（00:13:05）第二种，回到我们刚才讨论的主题——打造人们愿意购买的产品。关键是得做出对的产品。第三种，创始人的职责。我们常开玩笑说，更多公司死于自杀而非他杀。这听起来很残酷，但如果负责公司的两三个人无法和谐共事，其他一切都无从谈起。整个局面都会分崩离析。第四种，执行力。这里又回到了CEO的角色。好的，现在我们有了一堆比较幽默的例子。比如“机器人CEO”，他们认为创业公司不应该有任何情绪波动。对此，我们会用一个简单的公式来培训他们：情绪会带来混乱，人有情绪，创业公司需要人性化，所以创业公司注定是混乱的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how engineering-oriented that advice is, which makes sense for robots. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种以工程思维为主的建议，这对机器人来说确实适用。是啊。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: Also, a little bit more graceful of an answer there is also our CEOs want urgency and passion and excitement from their teams. They want them working enormously hard for below market comp more often than not with this promise of equity that might return value five or 10 or 12 years later. They want them to bring all of that emotion, but they're supposed to figure out how to surgically cut off the emotions that are inconvenient. That's the robot CEO who believes that we can just have several robots working for us and you just press a button and they do a thing. Second one is a pleaser CEO. This is the person who is far more concerned with being liked than running a business, so they can't tell anyone hard news. They can't break ties, they want a consensus on everything, and that's not possible. (00:14:56): If you have a group of thoughtful people working for you, they're going to fight, they're going to debate and you want them to. Then at some point you have to call it and say, "No, we're going left not right." Or, "The two of you need to go get in a room and deal with something." Or, "Hey, the way you just showed up is not the way I want you to show up." The pleaser CEO won't do any of that. They will simply hide and pray It goes away and it won't go away. Next one is a perfectionist CEO. I'd like to say that these are the CEOs with the most beautiful product to be delivered minutes before they file for bankruptcy. This is the person who is far more concerned with being right and believing that there's always a right answer than just moving forward. (00:15:36): It creates two problems in a business. One is you're just slow and the other one is you'll never take any bets because you will build a team that realizes the CEO is not allowed to be wrong, so you can't disagree, you can't use intuition, you can't use gut. Everything has to be utterly factual and that is simply not possible. In early-stage startups, you have more questions than you do answers. Everything is circumstantial. It's not like watching CSI entrepreneurship and you get to see a video to say, "Oh, look, the guy did it." No, we have a bunch of little data points you have to come to a conclusion. The next one is the angry CEO. (00:16:15): I had a founder of mine a bunch of years ago and we were seeing a pattern across the leadership team and he and I get on the phone one morning and I said, "I have a theory for you. It might be a story, I might be wrong, but I want to share." He said, " Okay." I said, "I think you wake up in the morning angry and you don't know it, and then you get to the office and you beat the crap out of the first employee that crosses paths with you over something utterly unrelated because you're angry. You realize that a few hours later and you apologize and your team hasn't quit yet because they believe you're a good human who doesn't have good self-control." Then I shared with him, "And you just had your first child. My guess is because I'm not a psychologist, I'm not a therapist, that you are modeling something that's happened in your life. Is this something you want to change?" (00:17:09): His answer is yes, and I said, "Great. I have good news and bad news. The good news is because you said yes, we can do something about it, and the bad news is I don't know what to fucking do. That's not my job." The point being, no one wants to work for the angry person. I don't care what the equity potential is worth, no one wants to work for that person, and the moment they see greener pastures elsewhere, they're leaving. The next one is the one that drives me particularly crazy, it's the laissez-faire CEO, who insanely believes that I can just hire great people and utterly ignore them and let markets take care of themselves and they will do all the right things. I have never met anyone, Lenny, that didn't benefit from good management and the laissez-faire CEO believes that management is not required, and so what they ultimately find is they have really, really good people doing utterly disconnected things and goals are not achieved. (00:17:59): Every CEO we can reductively reduce to one of two characters. They're either comfortable with the brake or comfortable with the accelerator. The challenge with those who are comfortable with the brake, what I mean by that is they don't want to spend any money, so they're driving this beautiful sports car and they're just leaning on the brake the whole time. Yes, they won't run any money, and yes, they will also get lapped by everyone else and miss the opportunity. Where their opportunity is, is where can you take bets? Where can you actually downshift that car in such a way where you give yourself a chance in the market? Separate, those who ride the accelerator, we've all met this one. They're going to run out of money really fast, and this connects to one of our other challenging CEO types, the ready, fire, aim. (00:18:49): Most CEOs are really bad at planning and that's because there's this little-known secret in the Bay area, most CEOs have never run a business before. Planning doesn't have to be some heavy bureaucratic multi-month exercise that begins in August and ends in February, but a little bit of bottoms up planning to say, what are we trying to achieve? How do we quantify it? What resources are required? What humans are going to do what? How do we shorten feedback loops so we know in a week, in a month and two months, whether we're on the right trajectory? The ready, fire, aim CEO says, "I don't want to do any of that because they're improvisational and they just want to take bets and they want to take shots," and that's what got the company started, and that's also what will have the company go bankrupt. The micromanager one is the opposite of laissez-faire. They believe that no matter how many employees they have, they can do the job better. (00:19:42): The challenge with this one is it is massively disrespectful to those who work for you. We think that, and this is a bit insulting, that everyone that works for a founder can be fit into one or two chunks. They're either an adult or a child. I have a three-year-old, my little girl is amazing. I'm utterly in love. If she doesn't have a lot of structure and a lot of supervision, she's going to run into things, man. Into things, off things, through things, but adults don't need to be given utter instruction and watched all the time. In fact, it needs to be the opposite. We agree on what success is, what resources are, and you let them go and they'll come back to you when they have questions. The micromanager CEO doesn't see the difference between those two humans. They don't trust anybody and that's actually the thing under the thing under the thing, so they want to do everyone's work and that will succeed right up into the point everyone quits.
turns.zh:
另外，一种更优雅的回答是，我们的CEO们希望团队充满紧迫感、激情和热情。他们希望团队成员能为低于市场水平的薪酬拼尽全力，而换来的股权可能要等五年、十年甚至更久才能变现。他们需要员工全情投入，但又必须学会如何冷酷地切断那些不利的情绪。这就是机器人式CEO，他们相信只要让多个机器人为我们工作，然后按个按钮就能完成任务。  

第二种是讨好型CEO。这种人更在意被他人喜欢，而非经营业务，因此无法向员工传递坏消息。他们无法果断裁员，事事都要达成共识，但这根本行不通。（00:14:56）：如果你手下有善于思考的员工，他们会激烈争论和辩论，而你需要适时做出决定。比如“不，我们要向左走而不是向右”；“你们俩得去闭门商量解决问题”；“你刚才的表现完全不符合我的期望”。讨好型CEO绝不会这样做，他们只会躲避问题，祈祷问题自行消失，但最终问题只会越积越多。  

第三种是完美主义CEO。我想说，这类CEO往往在破产前几分钟才推出最漂亮的产品。他们更执着于“正确答案”，总认为有唯一正确的解决方案，进而导致行动迟缓且不愿承担风险。他们组建的团队会认为CEO不可犯错，因此无法提出异议、运用直觉或凭感觉做决策，一切必须基于铁证。这在初创公司尤其明显——这里问题多于答案，一切都是推测，不像《犯罪现场调查》式的创业剧能通过视频证据定罪。这里只有零星数据点需要你自己得出结论。  

接下来是易怒型CEO。（00:16:15）：多年前我指导的一位创始人，我们发现整个领导团队都有这个问题。一天早上我们通话时，我说：“我有个推测，可能是个故事，也许错了，但想分享一下。”他说：“好。”我说：“你早上醒来时情绪低落，自己都没意识到，到办公室后因为一点无关紧要的事对第一个员工大发雷霆。几小时后你道歉，但团队还没离职，因为他们相信你是个善良但缺乏自控力的人。”然后我问：“你刚有了第一个孩子。虽说我不是心理学家或治疗师，但我猜这可能源于你生活中的某个经历。你想改变吗？” （00:17:09）：他回答想改。我说：“太好了。我有好消息和坏消息。好消息是既然你愿意改变，我们可以一起努力；坏消息是我不知道该怎么做。这不是我的职责。” 关键是，没人想为易怒的人工作。无论股权潜力多高，都没人愿意为他们工作，稍有风吹草动他们就会跳槽。  

接下来是……
尤其让我抓狂的是，那些奉行放任式管理的CEO。他们疯狂地认为，只要招来优秀人才，完全忽视他们的工作，任由市场自行调节，所有事情就会自然而然地做好。我从未遇到过一个例外的人，莱尼——任何人都受益于良好的管理。而放任式CEO却认为管理根本不需要，因此最终只能眼睁睁看着优秀人才各自为政，目标无法达成。（00:17:59）  

我们可以把所有CEO归结为两种类型：要么善于踩刹车，要么善于踩油门。善于踩刹车的人，也就是那些不愿花钱的CEO。他们开着豪华跑车，却始终踩着刹车不放。是的，他们省下了钱，但也会被其他人远远甩在身后，错失良机。他们的机会在于何处？在于何时敢于冒险？何时能让车子降档，为自己在市场中争取机会？  

至于踩油门的CEO，我们都遇到过这种人。他们会很快烧光资金，而这与另一种具有挑战性的CEO类型——"先开枪再瞄准"如出一辙。（00:18:49）  

大多数CEO规划能力薄弱，原因在于湾区有个鲜为人知的秘密：他们大多从未真正经营过企业。规划不必是那种从八月开始到二月结束的冗长官僚程序，而应是自下而上的小范围规划：我们要达成什么目标？如何量化？需要哪些资源？各岗位人员该做什么？如何缩短反馈周期，以便每周、每月、每季度都能判断是否方向正确？  

放任式CEO会说：“我才不想做这些，那太死板了。我要随机应变，放手一搏。”这或许成就了公司，但也可能导致其倒闭。  

微观管理型CEO与放任式恰恰相反。他们坚信无论员工多少，自己都能把工作做得更好。  

（00:19:42）  
这种管理者的挑战在于，他们对员工极度不尊重。我们会认为（这种说法略带贬义），所有为创始人工作的员工都可以归为两类：要么像孩子，要么像成人。我有个三岁的女儿，聪明极了。我对她宠爱有加。但如果没有严格的规矩和监督，她就会到处乱跑。成人不需要被时刻管控，恰恰相反。我们要明确成功标准和资源配置，放手让他们去行动，有问题再来找你。而微观管理型CEO看不到这两类员工的区别。他们不信任任何人，骨子里缺乏信任，因此想把所有工作都揽在自己手里，直到所有人离职为止。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is amazing. Okay, so let me recap these labels that you have just for folks. I have them written down here. There's the robot CEO, perfectionist CEO, pleaser CEO, micromanager, laissez-faire, ready, fire, aim, riding the brake and then riding the gas, and as you said, the ever-popular angry CEO.
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。好的，让我来总结一下你刚刚提到的这些领导者标签。我把它们都记下来了。有机器人CEO、完美主义CEO、讨好型CEO、微管理者、放任型、急于求成、犹豫不决、犹豫再行动，以及你提到的那个广受欢迎的"愤怒CEO"。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: You got them all.
turns.zh: 你把它们都列出来了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As people hear this, I imagine people self-identify a few of these, like I have some of this, I have some of that, and it's not like black or white. No one is like, "I'm a 100% robot CEO, and I need to fix that." It's like a pie chart kind of, I don't know, what's a visual of this? Everyone's got a little bit of this, basically.
turns.zh: 我觉得听众听完这些标签后，很多人会自我认同其中的某几个，比如“我有一些这样的特质，也有一些那样的特质”。这些特质并非非黑即白。没人会说：“我百分之百是机器人CEO，我必须改掉这个毛病。”这就像一个饼图，嗯，该怎么形象地展示呢？基本上每个人身上都会有这些特质的影子。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: That's right. I enjoy giving this talk on stage and watching different founders in the audience cringe at different moments, but it doesn't mean that they're all one or the other. If they were all one of these and then didn't want to even accept the possibility that there's a little bit of a lot of these that they could work on, they're probably not coachable and they're not going to be in the talk anyway.
turns.zh: 没错。我很享受在台上分享这些内容，看着台下不同的创始人在不同时刻露出不自在的表情，但这并不意味着他们非此即彼。如果他们完全符合某个标签，却不愿意承认自己身上也存在其他特质需要改进，那他们可能很难接受指导，也不适合参加这样的分享会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like I imagine each of these is very particular and it's this journey you go on to work on yourself. Let me just ask, what's the most common issue that you've found across these labels of type CEOs? What's the most common one and what do you often recommend someone to work on specifically to help them through that?
turns.zh: 我觉得每个标签都非常具体，改进自己就是一个持续的旅程。我想问一下，在这些CEO类型标签中，你发现最常见的问题是什么？最常见的问题是什么？针对这些问题，你通常会给出哪些具体的改进建议来帮助他们克服难关？

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: I think ready, fire, aim is the most common that we've seen, and that has been an affliction that's been growing in the last number of years. It wasn't long ago that CEOs could paper over poor execution with easy access to capital. Suddenly, over the last number of years, we're expecting founders to be better operators. Better operators means eventually being on a path when more cash comes into the business and out of the business. That doesn't happen by accident. The ready, fire, aim CEO has probably suffered this pain where they took lots and lots of bets. Maybe they measured the outcome after the fact and they were wrong and they were wrong and they were wrong in ways that were expensive, and they've raised their hand to say, "I see it. I want to get better at this." Basic, basic business design and business planning is not some corporate effort. It's some thoughtful exercise that starts with what are we working backwards from? (00:23:02): Because in any given time, Lenny, companies are working backwards from one of four things, whether they like it or not. I am working backwards from an exit. I'm working backwards from a next fundraise. I'm working backwards from profitability or I'm working backwards from winding down. We don't talk about the fourth one that much, but I got to choose one. I got to choose the top of the mountain. More often than not, they're choosing a fundraise. Then we'll ask that founder, you know your market, you know your investors, you know the next set of investors, we've done some intel. What has to be true to unlock the next fundraise? That's a qualitative and quantitative answer, but we write it down. We need to get better at go to market. We need to land our first partner. We need to launch next iteration of the product and show this level of efficacy, engagement, what have you. Can we codify that? Yes. Can we talk through what actions would be required on what cadence to unlock that quantified set of results? Yes.
turns.zh: 我认为“先开枪，后瞄准”是我们最常看到的现象，而这种现象近年来愈发严重。不久前，首席执行官们还能用容易获得的资金来掩盖执行不力的问题。但过去几年，人们开始要求创始人成为更出色的运营者。成为更优秀的运营者意味着，当资金流入和流出企业时，企业必须走上可控的发展道路。这并非偶然。那些急于行事却又行事不力的首席执行官们，可能曾高风险押注多次。或许他们事后评估结果时发现自己一错再错，损失惨重，最终不得不承认：“我意识到问题所在，我要改进。”基础的商业设计和规划并非企业层面的刻意之举，而是从目标倒推的深思熟虑之举。（00:23:02）：因为在任何特定时期，莱尼，企业无论愿不愿意，都必须从四件事中倒推其目标。我倒推的是退出策略。我倒推的是下一轮融资。我倒推的是盈利目标，或者倒推的是逐步退出。我们不常谈论第四种情况，但我必须选择一种。我必须选择山顶那座峰。多数情况下，他们会选择融资。然后我们会问创始人：你了解你的市场，你了解你的投资者，你了解下一轮投资者，我们已经做了充分调研。要达成下一轮融资，哪些条件必须满足？这既是定性的，也是定量的，但我们会将其记录下来。我们需要在市场推广方面做得更好，需要敲定首个合作伙伴，需要推出产品的新版本，并展示出有效性、用户参与度等指标。我们能将这些转化为可量化的标准吗？可以。我们能否梳理出达成这些目标所需的行动步骤和节奏？可以。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: ... that quantified set of results? Yes. Do we understand what resources would be required to do those things? Recognize we might have to squint through some of it, but again, the answer is yes. [inaudible 00:24:13] now aimed. If we have a culture that has some accountability, that has a communication architecture, so there's some rituals about how we meet and how we share information and how we talk through problems, and how we work through bottlenecks, well, now we have a plan and now we have accountability. I now no longer have to just guess all the time. And this only works for the CEO who says, "My improvisational efforts got me here, but I don't think they'll get me there." (00:24:47): There's a guy I worked for a long time ago, and he had this phrase... He had like seven or eight phrases, he would use them over and over and over again. It was hard not to commit them all to memory, and one of them was, "If you keep doing what you're doing, you keep getting what you're getting." And for the ready, fire, aim folks who realize the weakness of that at scale, the way to counteract that, is to start with good planning.
turns.zh: ……这些可量化的目标？可以。我们是否清楚实现这些目标需要哪些资源？我们承认可能需要仔细分析，但答案是肯定的。[00:24:13]现在回到正题。如果我们拥有问责文化，拥有沟通架构——即关于如何开会、如何共享信息、如何解决问题、如何突破瓶颈的固定流程——那么我们就有了计划，也有了问责机制。我再也不必一直靠猜测了。而这只适用于那些承认“即兴发挥曾让我走到今天，但我认为它无法带我更远”的首席执行官。（00:24:47）：很久以前我曾为一位高管工作，他有七八句口头禅，重复到让人难免牢记其中一句：“如果你继续按老路走，就只能收获老成果。” 而那些意识到这种模式弊端的急于行事者，要从做好规划开始着手应对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that's the most common type of CO, when with Founder Mode, it feels like it just accelerates that further. The whole meme of Founder Mode, which are what makes you upset. Makes sense. Great. (00:25:26): Okay, so I love that you talked about exiting as basically one of these four working backwards paths, because that's where I wanted to go next. I want to talk about some of these specific frameworks and skills and methodologies that you teach, and one of them... I want to almost go to the end of selling your company. And the reason I'm excited to talk about this, is if you think about, and tell me if I'm wrong, but it feels like most startups that succeed end up selling their company. That's the most likely success, right?
turns.zh: 很有意思的是，创始人模式（Founder Mode）恰恰是出售公司最常见的类型。整个创始人模式的梗，正是让人们感到沮丧的地方。说得在理。好的。（00:25:26）：好的，我很高兴你提到退出基本上是四种反向路径之一，因为这正是我接下来想讨论的。我想谈谈你教授的一些具体框架、技能和方法，其中之一……我几乎想直接跳到出售公司的环节。之所以我很兴奋谈论这个话题，是因为如果你仔细想想（如果我理解错了请纠正我），大多数成功的初创公司最终都会出售自己的公司。这是最有可能成功的路径，对吧？

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: Yes, by far.
turns.zh: 是的，到目前为止。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. Yeah, because the other option is IPO or just run this privately forever. Or fail, basically, and fold. So of the successful options, the most common is selling. At the same time, founders have never done this before, they don't know what they're doing. The other side, often, has done it many times, and so it's a pretty treacherous and scary and high-stakes thing to do and to learn on the spot. And you've come up with this methodology that you call the Magic Box Paradigm that I love, that helps founders think about how to lead to a successful exit long term. Can you talk about what this is?
turns.zh: 好的。是的，因为另一种选择是上市，或者永远保持私有。或者最终失败倒闭。所以在成功的选项中，最常见的是出售公司。与此同时，创始人之前从未做过这件事，他们不知道该怎么做。而另一方往往多次参与过，所以这是一件相当危险、可怕且高风险的事情，必须即刻上手学习。而你提出的这个名为"魔术盒范式"的方法，我很喜欢，它帮助创始人思考如何长期实现成功退出。你能谈谈这个范式吗？

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: I can, and I want to give credit where it's due. There's a book by this name, it's called Magic Box Paradigm, written by an independent banker named Ezra Roizen. And the book's fantastic, and Ezra is fantastic. (00:26:46): What we've done, is we've operationalized it so that we could teach founders over, and over, and over again. If the founder wants to hire a banker for this particular process, because we're not bankers, we're not BD, we don't get paid that way, we're teachers. But if wanted to hire a banker, go hire Ezra. But the methodology itself is a inversion for how venture and venture boards have thought about startups being ready for sale for a long, long time. It's utterly counter to so much advice that founders have heard. There are two ways you can get acquired. This is purposely reductive. One is you put up a for-sale sign. This is a traditional sales process. You build a list of the companies that might want to acquire you. You figure out the categories of buyers, the companies there, the contact list within that. You ping them and say, "We're open to a transaction," or some euphemism the like. You contact them and say, "I'll give you some information now. Sign an NDA. Give me an indication of interest by this date." And you work through a process, and you pray you have more than one person at the end of the game, try and ratchet them up, sign a term sheet. They will then re-trade along the way, right up until the point you die and you hope you get a deal done.
turns.zh: 我可以，而且我要把功劳归于原作者。有一本同名的书，叫《魔术盒范式》，由一位名叫埃兹拉·罗伊森的独立银行家撰写。这本书非常棒，埃兹拉本人也很棒。（00:26:46）：我们所做的，是将其具体化，以便反复教导创始人。如果创始人想为这个特定过程聘请银行家——因为我们不是银行家，不是业务开发人员，我们的报酬方式不同，我们是教师——但如果他们想聘请银行家，就去找埃兹拉。但这个方法本身是对风险投资和风险投资委员会长期以来认为初创公司必须做好出售准备的观念的颠覆。它与创始人听过的许多建议完全背道而驰。收购有两种方式。这里故意简化一下。一种是挂出"出售"标志。这是传统的销售流程。你列出可能收购你的公司名单。确定买家类别、相关公司，并在其中建立联系名单。你联系他们，说：“我们愿意进行交易。”或者用类似委婉的说法。你联系他们，说：“我现在会提供一些信息。签署保密协议。在某个日期前给出兴趣信号。”然后你按照流程推进，祈祷最后不止一个潜在买家，努力将他们拉升，签署投资意向书。然后他们会一路重新谈判，直到交易完成的那一刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds very familiar.
turns.zh: 听起来很熟悉。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: And it's one that often will just hit the nervous system of any founder that's been through it a couple of times. Because man, is it a fraught exercise? What Magic Box argues, is that the best outcomes for early-stage startups don't happen that way. You're never for sale. In fact, you have seduced a buyer. You have brought someone in. And there are three stages to Magic Box work. There is learn the fantasy, there's prove the fantasy, and there's quantify the fantasy. (00:28:43): All right, so what the hell do I mean by a fantasy? You're an early-stage startup, and you meet a company that is in your space, in your vertical, what have you, and they're much more advanced than you. It's a large business. Generally speaking, another oversimplification here, large companies are interested in small companies because they're technology. And small companies are interested in large companies because they're distribution. And there's someone at the large company who becomes fascinated with you. (00:29:12): What's the fascination? What they see in their head is, "Oh, interesting. If I buy your company, this thing happens." The classic example of this is Instagram. This is the number one example of this. Lenny, do you remember how much revenue they had when they got acquired by now Meta?
turns.zh:
这种情况常常会让那些经历过几次此类折磨的创业者神经紧绷。说真的，这真是个令人焦虑的过程。Magic Box认为，对于早期初创公司而言，最理想的成果并非通过这种方式达成。你永远不该被收购。实际上，收购方是在引诱你加入。他们是被你吸引进来的。Magic Box的工作分为三个阶段：首先是构想阶段，然后是验证阶段，最后是量化阶段。  

（00:28:43）好吧，那我说的"构想"到底指什么？假设你是一家早期初创公司，遇到一家同行业、同领域的巨头公司。他们比你先进得多，规模庞大。通常来说，大型企业对小公司的兴趣主要在于技术，而小公司则看重大公司的分销渠道。当大公司的某位高管对你产生兴趣时，会发生什么？  

（00:29:12）他们脑海中浮现的是："哦，有意思。如果我收购你们公司，会有这样的结果。"Instagram就是典型案例。这是此类合作的头号范例。Lenny，你还记得Instagram被Facebook收购时的营收状况吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it was zero.
turns.zh: 我想当时营收为零。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: I think it was zero.
turns.zh: 还是零。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: Do you remember the acquisition price?
turns.zh: 你记得收购价吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A billion dollars, which was absurd at that point.
turns.zh: 一百亿美元，在当时简直高得离谱。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: There was no math Facebook could use, historically speaking, that would justify a billion dollars. It had to be a model on the future. This is Magic Box to a T. They had a fantasy that adding Instagram would expand ad revenue. They figured out some way to prove it. I'll explain more on what I mean by proof. And then their quantification was based on the future. And that's the difference between a Magic Box approach and traditional approaches. Traditional approaches are based on the past, Magic Box is on the future. (00:30:14): Let me tell a story. In one of our companies in construction tech, their technology was able to suck in video camera data from construction sites for project planning. No one was doing this yet. And the business was doing pretty well. We helped the founders launch the company. We got first product in market. We raised a couple of rounds of capital. The product mostly worked. But we weren't sure it was venture scale as we were going along. And we had some large construction tech companies and real estate companies and development companies leaning into us. And one particular company then said, "Huh, we're really good at construction planning, and we've collected all of this video data that we don't use at all." And the champion on the other side in the product org, he has a fantasy. "Oh, shit. We take your video analytics platform and plug it into what we do, and this is what happens to my business." (00:31:18): Now, the person on the other side is a person. And the reason I'm being specific about that, is because you don't sell to a company. Magic Box is about finding the person. You're finding the champion on the other side, the person who has motivated for their own reasons, career, money, reputation, what have you. They see the fantasy. They fall in love. And this person says, "I am in love with this idea. If I can grab security data into my product organization. Now I have to prove the fantasy." (00:31:53): What's different about a champion in this kind of process, is they want to find a way to say yes. They're not looking for a way to say no. And this brings us to the four characters you're going to meet along the path of Magic Box. There might be a fifth. You're going to meet your champion, you're going to meet your advocates, you're going to meet your blockers, and you're going to meet your buyer. You might meet Corp Dev along the way. (00:32:20): Let me talk about each of those folks. The champion is the one who's fallen in love. They're the ones with the fantasy. They're the ones who are arguing on your behalf. They're the ones fighting for you when you're not in the room. They are texting you, they're telling you things about the business that they're probably not supposed to tell you. (00:32:33): The buyer. All they care about is math. It might be a committee, it might be a group, the IC, the EC, the investment group, what have you. They're the ones who actually can sign off on a deal. They care about business case. (00:32:45): Advocates... Lenny, do you play chess?
turns.zh:
历史上，Facebook没有任何数学模型能证明其价值数十亿美元。这必须是基于未来的预测。这正是Magic Box的精髓所在。他们曾幻想收购Instagram能提升广告收入，并设法证明了这一点。我会详细解释所谓的“证明”概念。他们的量化评估完全基于未来预期——这正是Magic Box与传统方法的根本区别。传统方法基于过去经验，而Magic Box则着眼于未来趋势。

（00:30:14）让我举个例子。在我们投资的建筑科技公司中，他们的技术能从施工现场获取视频数据用于项目规划。当时无人能做到这一点，业务进展顺利。我们协助创始人创立公司，推出了首款产品，成功融资多轮资金，产品基本可用。然而随着项目推进，我们始终不确定其是否具备风险投资级别。虽然有大型建筑科技公司、房地产开发商对我们感兴趣，但其中一家巨头突然表示：“我们擅长施工规划，手头有大量未被充分利用的视频数据。”而产品团队中的核心人物深受启发：“哦，天哪！如果我们能将你们的视频分析平台整合到我们的业务体系里，业绩将突飞猛进。”

（00:31:18）对方的核心人物至关重要。我强调这一点是因为你卖给的不是公司，而是要找到对方的需求点。你要找到对方的推动者——那些出于个人动机（事业、金钱、声誉等）主动拥护新理念的人。他们心怀幻想，深深着迷，并会说：“我太爱这个创意了！如果能将安全数据整合到我的产品线中，就能验证这个愿景。”

（00:32:20）Magic Box流程中的四大角色分别是：推动者、拥护者、阻碍者和买家。途中可能还会遇到企业发展部门。

推动者：他们满怀热情，深信不疑，替你据理力争，帮你争取资源。

拥护者：他们积极支持，但不参与决策，默默为你传递关键信息。

阻碍者：他们固守传统思维，质疑商业逻辑，制造障碍。

买家：他们只看数字，关注商业案例，负责最终决策。

（00:32:45）拥护者……莱尼，你会下国际象棋吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have played chess, yes.
turns.zh: 我下过国际象棋的，是的。

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: You have played chess. So advocates are pawns. They don't matter at all until they matter enormously. These are folks that, like, you are the CEO doing a meeting with your potential buyer, and there are somehow 12 people on the Zoom call, but only two do the talking. The other 10 might be advocates. They're rooting for you, but they will take no political risk. Their value is in giving you intel. (00:33:16): Blocker. This is the person who can't say yes, but they can say no. This is OPSEC, this is Procurement, this is Legal. You're going to meet all these characters during the Magic Box dance. Your champion just wants you to get the deal done so in love. So what happens, is they've come up with a fantasy and you as a CEO need to lean into it. This isn't enterprise selling. I'm not trying to sell you this thing that I have. I'm just trying to find ways to say yes. (00:33:47): So when, in my story, the person says, "Could we provide you all of our video data that we've collected forever and you now could enhance our ability to predict whether large- scale construction projects are on time"? I don't want the CEO saying anything other than, "We can do that." (00:34:07): Now, phase two, I need to prove it. Okay, because I have a champion who wants to say yes, proof can be really easy. And the reason the proof is so important, is not to convince the champion they're in love with the fantasy. They're already convinced. It's because in almost all cases, big company is buying little company and your champion doesn't have unilateral authority. They're going to socialize the deal. They have to get buy-in from who? The aforementioned buyer. They have to be able to survive the aforementioned blockers. (00:34:43): So eventually, when they pitch this to whatever committee is in charge, that committee is going to say, "What proof do we have that it works?" And we just want to be able to provide the champion with enough evidence that it works. So in this case, we said to the champion, " Well, give us video data, and we will provide you the evidence that you need." Because we're dealing with a champion who's not a cynic, because champions aren't, we could tell them, "And provide us the data in this way, in this fashion, and here's what we'll send you after. Are we in agreement?" We know we're already going to win the proof, and it's critically important in these dances. (00:35:27): Number three, quantify. At this point, we're not up for sale, but we're spending a lot of calories on somebody, and they know it. So we have our CEOs say the following phrase to them: "My board is asking questions. They're wondering why we're spending so many calories on this when it's not really core and we're not selling you our product. I'm convinced of how exciting this could be, together, but I think we need to do some math. So I can explain to my board why this might matter. So let's imagine all this works, because it's going to work, and it's a year from now or five years from now. What changes about your business?" And the champion will tell you, "Retention does this, or deal size goes like this, or market share goes like this." And you'll say to them, "Fantastic. Look, I'm going to build some shitty verse version of the model. You tell me what I got right and what I got wrong, but I have a board meeting in 16 days, and I need to be able to walk them through the justify why I am spending so many calories on this exercise." (00:36:34): You build the model, you hand it to them. If they in any way respond to your model, you've won. Because you have now divorced history from future, and you are now playing in future, you are playing the Instagram game in this case. The ending of the story for the company that I was describing, it was a business sub 2 million in revenue. Our prospects of raising series B felt low. We were not yet profitable, and that was an exit that was generational wealth for the co-founders and their families. The CEO went on and spent two-plus years with the now public company that did this acquisition. The technology did get integrated, but it took a long time and they had to do a lot of changes to it, certainly beyond what was envisioned during the diligence process. But all parties are happy. And if we hadn't done it this way and we had just been up for sale, we'd get a dollar for that company. (00:37:40): A couple of other side points that are really important here. For any of you founders out there that are thinking about working backwards from an exit, there are two things that I really want to stress. One is the fantasy is beyond just, "What is the business change you can have?" The fantasy is, "Your books are in order." Your fantasy is all of your investors will sign off on the deal and you will have unanimous consent, that the key members of your team are going to stick around, that you're a joy to work with. Please God, founder, do not puncture the fantasy at any time. (00:38:21): So whatever is starting to shape in your buyer's mind, get to know it. Live that everybody wins from that game. Second, Corp Dev, they will probably show up in the stands. Corp Dev make deals. They're not deal sponsors, they're not a champion, they're not a buyer. They are an expert negotiator. Their job is to facilitate deals and get deals done. The most important things to understand is that they can be a leverage point to have a deal move with some process and some pace and some urgency. Because either deals have momentum or they die, and Corp Dev can help there. (00:39:04): Second, they are way better at negotiating than you. So anytime dealing with a superior negotiator, the only thing you can do to try and even the scales, is move the negotiation async. So founders, repeat after me, I'm talking to you directly now. You'll say to Corp Dev, "You know I'm not alone in this decision. I love what you just said and I'm excited about this opportunity. Once I see it in writing, I can socialize it with advisors, lawyers, co-founders, whoever." But don't negotiate live. You will lose.
turns.zh:
你玩过国际象棋吧。在那里，棋子都是步兵。直到它们变得至关重要之前，它们根本不算什么。就像你作为CEO与潜在买家开会时，Zoom通话里有12个人，但只有两人在发言。其他10个可能都是支持者。他们支持你，但不会承担政治风险。他们的价值在于提供情报。  
（00:33:16）：阻挠者。这类人无法说“是”，但能说“不”。比如OPSEC、采购部门、法务部。在“魔盒舞”中，你会遇到各种角色。你的支持者只想达成交易，所以你得顺应他们的幻想。这不是企业销售。我不是要推销自己的产品，而是想办法达成合作。  
（00:33:47）：那么在我的案例中，当对方问：“我们能否提供所有长期收集的视频数据，以提升大型建筑项目按时完工的预测能力？”CEO必须回答：“我们能做到。”  
（00:34:07）：第二阶段，我需要证明方案可行。因为支持者已经深陷幻想，证明过程至关重要。关键在于说服大公司收购小公司的团队，他们没有全权决策权，必须获得上级批准。  
（00:34:43）：最终，当方案提交给委员会时，他们会问：“有何证据证明方案有效？”我们让支持者提供视频数据，然后提供所需证据。  
（00:35:27）：第三步，量化收益。此时我们虽未达成交易，但已投入大量精力，对方心知肚明。我们让CEO对他们说：董事会质疑为何投入大量精力却非核心业务。支持者会列举业务改进，如留存率提升、交易规模增长等。这时我们会说：建个简化模型，告诉我们优缺点，16天后我要向董事会汇报投资理由。
来自未来——而你如今正身处未来，在这种情况下，你正在玩Instagram游戏。我所描述的那家公司的结局是，其营收不足200万美元。我们获得B轮融资的可能性很低，当时我们尚未实现盈利，但那对联合创始人及其家庭而言是一次能创造世代财富的退出机会。首席执行官随后加入了如今已上市的收购方公司。技术整合确实完成了，但过程漫长，且需要进行大量调整，远超尽职调查阶段的预期。不过各方最终皆大欢喜。如果我们当初没有选择这种退出方式，而是一味等待被收购，那家公司最终只能卖个白菜价。  

（00:37:40）还有几个至关重要的侧面观点。对于正在考虑从退出角度倒推的创业者们，我想强调两点：其一，幻想远不止于“业务能做出哪些改变”。幻想还包括“账务清晰无误”、所有投资者都同意交易、核心团队成员能留任、合作愉快等诸多要素。请千万别在任何时候戳破这个幻想。  

（00:38:21）其次，企业发展部门（Corp Dev）很可能会介入谈判。他们是交易推动者，而非交易发起者、支持者或买家。他们是专业谈判专家，职责是促成交易达成。关键在于，他们能通过施压手段推动交易进程，确保交易保持动力。因为交易要么势头正盛，要么胎死腹中，Corp Dev能在这方面发挥作用。  

（00:39:04）其次，他们的谈判能力远超你。所以面对更强硬的谈判对手时，唯一能扳回局面的方法就是异步谈判。创业者们，请听好：我现在直接对你们说。当你向Corp Dev表示“我不是唯一做决策的人”时，要保持礼貌，同时传递你的热情：“我很赞同你的提议，对这个机会充满期待。一旦收到书面协议，我会与顾问、律师、联合创始人等沟通。”但切勿当场签约，否则必败无疑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me just say that was extremely delightful to listen to. I've never heard like a M&A strategy be this fun. And it makes me want to sell a company. It's like, "Okay, let's do this. I'm hyped." I think you got it all. I have a few questions. (00:39:56): Interestingly, the middle part is... It feels a lot like enterprise sales, which a lot of founders are used to. Understand the stakeholders move things forward. Here's your champion, here's your blockers, here's the buyer. Is there anything there you want to say, what's maybe most different from enterprise sales, which I think a lot of founders are maybe used to? Or is it pretty similar?
turns.zh: 不得不说，这番讲解真是太精彩了。我从未听过如此生动的并购策略解析，简直让人听得热血沸腾，恨不得立刻就去出售公司。就像是：“好吧，让我们行动起来。我现在兴奋极了！” 我觉得你把所有关键点都讲透了。不过我还有几个问题想请教。（00:39:56）：有趣的是，中间那部分……感觉和企业销售很像，很多创始人都对此比较熟悉。理解各利益相关方的动向是推动进程的关键——这边是支持者，另一边是阻力者，还有买家。你们有没有什么不同于企业销售的独特之处？或者说两者其实很相似？

turns.speaker: Jonathan Lowenhar
turns.en: Yeah, I think three things. One is there are a lot of moments in enterprise sales where we're trying to push for a compelling event. That doesn't work in seduction. The playful metaphor that we'll often use, is you've been dating for a while, this person could be the person, but they're not quite convinced yet that it should be a life together, and you're sitting at dinner. And in enterprise sales, you're eager to get it done. You're eager to move the relationship forward and move in and get engaged, what have you. And so you might be inclined to say, "Hey, either we move this relationship the next step, or there are a whole bunch of people eyeing me, and I'm going to go date someone else." (00:41:06): That conversation never goes well, and in Magic Box founders are eager to do the same thing, thinking that competition will improve their deal size, when in fact I think more often than not, that is a negative signal until the very end of the dance. So instead in enterprise selling where I'm pushing, in Magic Box, I'm always trying to entice, I'm never, ever trying to push. So instead I might say things like, "Hey, I'm going to raise my next round in Q1, because I've been intending to do this business independently. Now all I really want to do, is win. I just want my product in as many customers' hands as possible. Whether I do that on my own as I was planning, in partnership with someone, or under someone else's roof, honestly I don't care. But I have a company to run and I'm going to go raise my next round in Q1. And if I do that, probably too expensive for this deal to make sense anymore, and my board will want me to move on anyway." I'm enticing. I'm never trying to push.
turns.zh: 是的，有三个关键点。首先，企业销售中有很多时候，我们需要推动达成一个关键协议。但这种策略在追求异性时并不适用。举个有趣的比喻：你和某人约会了一段时间，觉得对方可能就是命中注定，但对方还没完全下定决心要共度一生。你们共进晚餐时，你急切地想推进关系，迫切希望达成订婚等重大决定。而在企业销售中，你可能更倾向于说：“嘿，要么我们现在推进合作，要么就会有其他人盯上我，我得去和别人约会了。” （00:41:06）：这种谈判方式往往不顺利。在Magic Box，我们也遇到过类似的情况。创始人总想通过竞争来提升交易规模，但实际上，这种策略往往适得其反，直到交易的最终阶段才有所成效。所以在企业销售中，我会推动进程，而在Magic Box，我始终在引诱对方。我从不强行推进，而是会说：“嘿，我计划在第一季度完成下一轮融资，因为我一直打算独立运营这项业务。现在我唯一想做的，就是赢得胜利。我只想让尽可能多的客户使用我的产品。无论是独立发展、与他人合作，还是加入他人旗下，我都无所谓。但我得继续经营公司，所以必须在第一季度完成融资。如果融资失败，这笔交易可能就不划算了，董事会也会让我另谋出路。”这就是引诱，而不是强行推动。
